html:
The Pueblo peoples are the farming nations of the American Southwest who live in compact towns of stone and adobe, called pueblos by the Spanish. The map uses one wide shape for them in 1492, covering the Four Corners region of today's Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah.

They descend from the Ancestral Puebloans, who built the great houses of Chaco Canyon and the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde. Around 1300 drought and unrest drove people south and east, to the Hopi mesas, Zuni and the Rio Grande valley, where most pueblos still stand. They grew maize, beans, squash and cotton with careful water management, and held their religious life in round underground rooms called kivas.

  • Hopi and Zuni in the west; Acoma, Laguna and the Keres towns in the middle; Tewa, Tiwa and Towa towns on the Rio Grande.
  • Acoma and Taos are among the oldest continuously lived in towns in North America.

The Spanish came with Coronado in 1540 and settled in 1598 as part of New Spain. Forced labour and attacks on their religion led to the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, which drove the Spanish out for twelve years. Their neighbours, the Navajo and Apache, were sometimes trading partners and sometimes raiders. Nineteen pueblos in New Mexico and the Hopi in Arizona remain self governing today.
